### Question and data (15%)

- [ ] The blog post provides context and background for the question
- [ ] The data are explained using text and figures
- [ ] The theorized causal relationships are described with a DAG

Kelp forests play important roles in preserving global biodiversity, performing ocean carbon (CO2) absorption, providing biomass and nursery habitats related to the fishing industry, and protecting coastline communities from erosion effects. There is an assumption in some policy and scientific communities that MPAs - originally designed to conserve kelp forest ecosystems and rebuild fishery habitats after overfishing events - also protect these ecological communities from the effects of climate change (i.e. MHW-caused damage). Many global communities rely on fishing economies, and if negative effects from MHWs and other climate change-related events are, in fact, being ameliorated by the existance of MPAs, that would be great. However, there appears to be disagreement in scientific and policy opinions on whether or not there is evidence that MPAs render any positive effect on California kelp forest communities. If another type of ecosystem remediation is needed to protect essential kelp forest communities from MHWs, this needs to be identified.

State Marine Reserve (SMR) prohibits all take or damage of marine resources, while a State Marine Conservation Area (SMCA) allows specific commercial or recreational take

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  %% Water temp affects nutrient and prey availability for predator species
  water_temp --> species_richness
  %% PH affects nutrient and prey availability for predator species
  pH --> species_richness
  %% MPA_status affects fishing/harvesting/outside access which impacts species richness
  MPA_status --> species_richness
  %% Pollution can make water more or less acidic depending on the pollution type
  pollution --> pH
  %% Pollution can introduce poisons to the ecosystem
  pollution --> species_richness
  %% Climate change effects can reduce the number of species
  climate change --> species_richness
  %% Climate change effects can increase water temp
  climate change --> water_temp
```

Pollution and pH are not in my dataset, which could introduce bias into my results as both have potentially major effects on species survivability in kelp forests. Water temp (w/ 38% missing data) and climate change/MHW (through years and dates) are in my dataset.

Question: Did kelp forests in Southern California long-term marine protected areas (MPAs) have better resistance to the 2014-2016 marine heatwave (MHW) than unprotected Southern California Kelp Forests? Resistance defined as less change in the observed statistic (biomass/fish count or type count/pct canopy) from before (2011-2013) to during (2014-2016) and during to after (2017-2019).

### Statistical model (35%)

- [ ] The statistical model is explained conceptually and using formal statistical notation
- [ ] The choice of model is justified based on the characteristics of the data and model assumptions
- [ ] Potential limitations of the model and data are considered

```{r}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(ggpubr)
library(MASS)
```

```{r}
# Load data
# Fish transect-level survey
fish_df <- read_csv(here('EDS222_KelpForestMPAs','data','PISCO_kelpforest_fish.1.11.csv'))
# Site table (MPA status)
site_df <- read_csv(here('EDS222_KelpForestMPAs','data','PISCO_kelpforest_site_table.1.11.csv'))
# Taxa table (Classcode definition)
taxa_df <- read_csv(here('EDS222_KelpForestMPAs','data','PISCO_kelpforest_taxon_table.1.11.csv'))
```

```{r}
# Find columns to merge on btwn fish and site dfs
shared_cols_fish <- intersect(colnames(fish_df), colnames(site_df))
# print(shared_cols_fish)

# Filter sites df before join
site_filt_df <- site_df |> 
                # Keep Southern CA sites and remove any site_status "N/A"s
                filter((campus == "UCSB") & (site_status %in% c("mpa","reference"))) |> 
                # Group by site (site name), site_status (site type - mpa or reference)
                group_by(site, site_status) |>  
                # Remove duplicate rows - only need one row per site, site_status
                slice(1) |> 
                ungroup() |> 
                # Keep relevant columns in site df for mpa/ref status labeling of fish_df
                select(site, MPA_Name, mpa_type, site_status)

# Merge mpa status to fish df
fish_mpa_df <- fish_df |> 
                # Filter to relevant years, Southern CA
                filter((survey_year >= 2011) & (survey_year <= 2019) & (campus == "UCSB")) |> 
                # Remove unecessary and duplicate columns
                select(-campus,-year,-method) |> 
                # Join to site_filt_df to label mpa/ref sites
                inner_join(site_filt_df,
                           by = join_by(site)
                           ) |> 
                # Remove MPAs without a type (only SMR or SMCA)
                filter(mpa_type != "N/A") |> 
                # Create MHW year categories
                mutate(MHW_Category = ifelse(
                            (survey_year >= 2014 & survey_year <= 2016),
                            "During",
                            ifelse(
                                (survey_year >= 2017),
                                "After",
                                "Before"
                            )
                )) |> 
                mutate(MHW_Category = factor(MHW_Category, levels = c("Before", "During", "After"))) |> 
                # Calculate species richness (row count) and total biomass_g (sum row_weight_g) per site, site_status, year, month combo
                summarise(species_richness = n_distinct(classcode),
                          total_biomass_g = sum(row_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE),
                          mean_temp_C = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
                          n_transects = n_distinct(paste(day, zone, level, transect)),
                          .by = c(survey_year, month, MPA_Name, mpa_type, site_status, MHW_Category))
```

# Poisson - Species Richness

Scientific Hypothesis: Kelp forests in long-term MPAs in Southern California had better resilience to the 2014-2016 MHW event than unprotected Southern California kelp forests.

Statistical H_null: MPA status had no effect on species richness before, during, or after the 2014-2017 MHW in Southern California.

Statistical H_alt: Kelp forests in Southern California MPAs had less change in species richness before, during, and after the 2014-2016 MHW compared to unprotected Southern California kelp forests.

1. Visualize the data
2. Fit the model
3. Interpret the coefficients
4. Convert log counts to counts
5. Visualize the predictions

## Visualize the data

Each row is contains measurements at a single site in a single month. `species_richness` is the number of species recorded in the month at that site. `mean_temp_C` is the mean water temperature in degrees C for that month at that site.

## Fit the model

The model in statistical notation is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{SpeciesRichness} &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) \\
\log(\lambda) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{MHW} + \beta_2 \text{MPA} + \beta_3 (\text{MHW} * \text{MPA})
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
# Fit Poisson model: species_richness ~ mean_temp_C * site_status and offset (coef = 1) accounting for the number of transects per site measured
sr_p_mpa_glm <- glm(species_richness ~ MHW_Category * site_status + offset(log(n_transects)), family = poisson(link = "log"), data = fish_mpa_df)
```

```{r}
# Fit NegBin model: species_richness ~ mean_temp_C * site_status and offset (coef = 1) accounting for the number of transects per site measured

sr_nb_mpa_glm <- glm.nb(species_richness ~ MHW_Category * site_status + offset(log(n_transects)), data = fish_mpa_df)
```

## Interpret the coefficients

```{r}
# Poisson model summary
summary(sr_p_mpa_glm)
# Check dispersion statistic - sum(residuals^2) / n - k
pois_disp_stat = sum(residuals(sr_p_mpa_glm)^2) / df.residual(sr_p_mpa_glm)
# pois_disp_stat = 4.42, much larger than 1 so data is overdispersed and NegBin will be used
```

```{r}
# NegBin model sumary
summary(sr_nb_mpa_glm)
```

Each percentage point of impervious surface changes the _log_ of the expected number of exotic species by 0.0125.

Exponentiate the coefficients to put them on the count scale.

```{r}
exp(coef(sr_nb_mpa_glm))
```

Each percentage point of impervious surface _multiplies_ the expected number of exotic species by 1.0126 (1.3% increase). 

## Convert log counts to counts

First, create a _prediction grid_ covering the range of the predictor.

```{r}
# Create prediction grid with all possible predictor combos, all to predict a species richness count in 1 transect
sr_mpa_pred_grid <- expand_grid(
  MHW_Category = factor(c("Before", "During", "After"), levels = c("Before", "During", "After")),
  site_status = c("mpa","reference"),
  n_transects = 1
)
```

Next, use `predict()` to get the expected species richness, $\lambda$. `type = "response"` gives $\lambda$; `type = "link"` would give $\log(\lambda)$.

```{r}
sr_mpa_pred_grid$lambda <- predict(
  sr_nb_mpa_glm,
  type = 'response',
  newdata = sr_mpa_pred_grid
)
```

## Visualize the predictions

Overlay the expected counts on the raw data.

```{r}
# Boxplot plot - MHW_Category vs species richness

sr_mpa_pred_grid$`Site Status` <- sr_mpa_pred_grid$site_status

fish_mpa_df |> 
  mutate(`Site Status` = site_status) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = MHW_Category, y = species_richness/n_transects, fill = `Site Status`)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  geom_line(
    data = sr_mpa_pred_grid,
    aes(y = lambda, group = `Site Status`, color = `Site Status`),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = sr_mpa_pred_grid,
    aes(y = lambda, group = `Site Status`, color = `Site Status`),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
    labs(x = "MHW Category",
         y = "Species Richness / Number of Transects",
         title = "Effect of MHW and MPA Status on Species Richness")
```
